newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Navy analyst charged with spying for S. Korea.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Navy analyst charged with spying for S. Korea.

text.p: A computer specialist for a U.S. Navy intelligence agency has been arrested on espionage charges for passing secret and top-secret documents to a South Korean Embassy official, the FBI said on Wednesday.

It said Robert Kim, 56, an 18-year government employee who worked at a U.S. Navy intelligence office in Suitland, Maryland, was arrested without incident Tuesday night at a diplomatic reception at Fort Myer, Virginia.
Kim was charged with passing classified information to a South Korean agent, a naval attache at the embassy in Washington identified as Capt. Dong-Il Baek.
Baek's office declined to comment, but a Justice Department source said the naval officer, who arrived in 1994 for a three-year tour, would soon leave the United States for Seoul.

At a five-minute court hearing in Alexandria, Virginia, prosecutor Robert Chestnut said Kim should be held in jail without bail "because of his close relationship with Korea, there is a serious risk of flight."

Jim Clark, a court-appointed defence lawyer, replied that Kim's wife and son live in the area and denying him bond "unfairly prejudges Mr. Kim." A federal magistrate set a new hearing for Monday on whether Kim should be held without bond.
Kim, of Sterling, Virginia, was born in Seoul and became a U.S. citizen in 1974. He was charged with passing the classified information from May through September.
FBI agent Gloria Harbold said in a 21-page affidavit that Kim regularly searched the Navy intelligence computer system for secret and top-secret documents.
"Kim copies and stores these documents in his work computer, removes classification markings and prints them on his office printer and transmits them to Baek," she said.
Harbold said investigators obtained evidence against Kim from electronic and video surveillance, and searches at work and his mail.

She said the FBI on May 5 seached his work computer, finding a file containing a letter dated Jan. 24, 1996, in which Kim offered his services to Baek. Kim said he hoped Baek had digested "the materials I have sent you" and warns him to "please be careful."
Harbold said Kim had stored in his computer a number of "K" files containing U.S. government documents on North and South Korea and other Asian-Pacific countries.

On May 10, electronic surveillance revealed Kim telephoned Baek and Baek confirmed he received "it" -- an apparent reference to a package of several classified documents. Baek added, "You don't know much much I treasure this."

Harbold said the FBI on several occasions in August and September even intercepted envelopes Kim had mailed to Baek, opened them to find various classified documents, and then allowed all but a few of the documents to be received.
The FBI said its surveillance revealed Kim playing golf at a course in Fort Meade, Maryland, with Baek and two high-ranking South Korean naval officials.

"I know that Kim has used his vehicle and briefcase to transport classified documents from his office to his home and to the home of Captain Baek. Kim has also used manila envelopes and stamps that Baek provided him with return address labels," Harbold said.

A Justice Department official said the case was much less signficant than the scandal involving former Central Intelligence Agency agent Aldrich Ames, who was sentenced to life in prison for spying for Moscow for $2.5 million.
Kim was charged under an espionage law that carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison, the official said.
Clinton administration officials said they were disturbed by the incident but it was unlikely to affect U.S.-Korea ties.

"Relations between the United States and the Republic of Korea are strong and of the nature that they can endure any alleged wrongdoing by an individual," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher said he was very disturbed by Kim's arrest and said Washington had been in touch with South Korean officials over the case.
